result.summary: Pausanias sketches the early career of Epaminondas and tells how Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra. The Spartans suffer bad omens and the old wrong done to the daughters of Scedasus, and Epaminondas wins a decisive victory.

scenes.title: Epaminondas' youth and embassy
scenes.summary: Epaminondas' education, his rescue of Pelopidas, and his reply to Agesilaus at Sparta about the peace.
scenes.stakes: Epaminondas risks his life saving Pelopidas and defends Theban claims over Boeotia.

scenes.title: Invasion and omens
scenes.summary: Cleombrotus bypasses Epaminondas, reaches Leuctra, and wolves kill the goats leading the Spartan flocks.
scenes.stakes: Sparta's army faces defeat, foretold by ill omens.

scenes.title: Daughters of Scedasus
scenes.summary: Two Spartans rape Scedasus' daughters, who hang themselves; Scedasus kills himself and Epaminondas honors them and vows battle.
scenes.stakes: The daughters and Scedasus suffer an unavenged outrage and lose their lives.

scenes.title: Boeotarchs decide for battle
scenes.summary: The Boeotarchs split three to three until Bacchylides votes for battle; Epaminondas sends doubtful allies home.
scenes.stakes: Thebes risks defeat and siege if the decision is wrong.

scenes.title: Battle of Leuctra
scenes.summary: Thebes defeats Sparta; Cleombrotus falls, and Epaminondas has the allies bury their dead first, exposing Spartan losses.
scenes.stakes: Thebes risks its country, wives and children; Sparta its prestige and king's body.

characters.name: Scedasus
characters.description: Man of Leuctra who killed himself

characters.name: Bacchylides
characters.description: Seventh Boeotarch, casting vote for battle

notable_quotes.reason: Epaminondas' sharp reply to Agesilaus on Boeotian towns and Spartan neighbours.
Pausanias judges Leuctra the most notable Greek victory over Greeks.

analysis.text: Pausanias links Sparta's defeat to divine omens and to vengeance for a wrong, showing moral causes behind military outcomes.
Leuctra (371 BC) ended Spartan dominance and began a brief period of Theban supremacy in Greece.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias' figures, 47 Theban dead against over 1,000 Spartans, are far lower than the Spartan losses usually cited elsewhere, which include about 400 Spartiates.

language_notes.text: The peace of Antalcidas (387 BC), the King's Peace, required Greek cities to be autonomous, which would break up Theban leadership of the Boeotian towns.
"Turned aside to Ambrosus" means Cleombrotus took a different route through Phocis, avoiding the forces Epaminondas had posted at the marsh.
_Catoiades_ is a Greek term for a particular kind of goat; Pausanias gives no more detail about it.
Refers to the story of Scedasus' daughters, told in the following sentences; their rape is presented as the cause of Spartan punishment at Leuctra.
Bœotarchs were the chief officers of the Boeotian federation, who commanded its army and decided policy.
"Whoever would" means anyone who wished; Epaminondas removed unreliable troops rather than risk desertion in the battle.

context_notes.text: Epaminondas became the great Theban general and statesman. Pythagoras' followers were known for philosophy, discipline and mathematics.
Sacrificing animals before battle was standard Greek practice; the omens from the victims guided commanders' decisions.
Spartan citizens were few and prized, so heavy losses among them were a serious blow to Sparta.

literary_notes.text: Epaminondas' sharp retort shows his boldness and his political skill, turning Sparta's own demand against it.
The wolves killing the goats that lead the flocks is an omen of the Spartan defeat to come.
Sparta's habit of hiding its losses is used against it, as the allies' burials reveal the truth.
